title: NFL bans misleading scoreboard images during kicks
seoTitle: NFL bans misleading scoreboard images during kicks
subtitle: New rule prevents teams from showing different angles on videoboards during field goals and extra points
excerpt: The league changed how scoreboards can be used during kicks after a Patriots trick was revealed, requiring a single image for both teams.
author: Daniele Morais
contentHtml:
The revelation of a visual trick used by the New England Patriots during field goal and extra point kicks generated significant buzz and led the league to change its videoboard rules. The trick was disclosed by Ryan Paganetti, a former analytics coach, who shared images showing the scoreboard displaying a second, offset set of yellow uprights.

Trick discovered in Patriots games

Paganetti analyzed more than ten years of Patriots broadcasts and shared screenshots on social media in which the videoboard displayed a mirrored view of the kick attempt, with yellow uprights positioned behind the real ones. In windy conditions, even the orange ribbons on the scoreboard pointed in the opposite direction, enhancing the illusion.

New NFL rule for videoboards

In a memorandum sent to all teams on September 7, the NFL ruled that during field goal and extra point attempts, all teams must use the same "All-22" image—a high-angle shot from the sideline or end zone—or a static image. Displaying different images for each team will no longer be permitted.

How the All-22 image works

The All-22 feed corresponds to a camera positioned at an elevated angle, showing the entire field uniformly. This view was already required to prevent lighting effects, flashing text, or moving videos during kicks, but it must now be identical for both teams.

Team reactions and potential impacts

With the change, teams will need to find other ways to gain a competitive advantage, as they will no longer be able to manipulate opponents' perception through the videoboard. The league emphasized that the Patriots operated within the rules in effect at the time.

With information from the New York Post, Bleacher Report.
